name: PT Bank Ina Perdana Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Ina Perdana: a small bank carrying a group premium
frontmatter.summary: Bank Ina earns a return on equity far below its cost of equity, has just cleaned up its loan book and is raising capital from its controlling shareholder at the market price. The shares trade at a large multiple of the book value those returns support. We initiate at SELL: even after crediting most of the Salim-group premium to the target, the twelve-month return is negative.
thesis: SELL, target Rp2,093, a -42.5% total return with no dividend (Rp0). Fundamental value is Rp86; the Rp3,640 price is 6.6x FY2026E book against a justified 0.3x.

The gap is structural. We build a sustainable ROE of 6.2% against a 12.5% cost of equity: the margin recovers only to 2.6%, the cost base falls to 66.0% of income and credit cost normalises to 1.1% [S7][S8]. No plausible mix of those three closes the gap to the cost of equity.

The FY2025 loss was a genuine clean-up, not a one-off to be ignored: provisions of IDR602.0bn and write-offs of IDR431.0bn cut gross NPL to 3.0% [S8]. But the book has already rebuilt to 4.0% gross and 12.4% low-quality, with the allowance at 93.0% of the regulatory minimum [S7][S6].

This is a group-funded balance sheet. Related parties placed IDR5,860.0bn of third-party funds at end-2025 [S8], and the controlling shareholder has just bought more stock at the market price (Rp3,620, IDR50.0bn raised) with a second tranche of up to 350m shares announced and unpriced [S5][S3].

The price is a regime, not a valuation: it sits at 47.7x our fundamental value on the house konglo registry. Our target already assumes most of that premium survives twelve months; the bear and bull regime cases are Rp226 and Rp6,028.
What would change the rating: a stage II placement priced well above the market, four quarters of credit cost at the 2026 run-rate, or a binding offer for control of the bank.

catalysts.event: Stage II private placement: exercise price, timetable and allocation to the Anthoni Salim entities
FY2026 audited results and the fourth-quarter provision charge
Annual report and AGMS: dividend, further capital raise, any change in group ownership
First-quarter LK: NPL, allowance against the regulatory minimum, CASA and margin
Free-float transition date for smaller issuers; BINA's float already clears the minimum
MSCI consultation feedback closes on the Standalone-market proposal
MSCI decision on reclassifying Indonesia to Standalone Market status
Free-float transition date: the full minimum applies to all listed issuers; BINA is already compliant

blocks.text: Bank Ina Perdana is a small, group-funded Indonesian bank whose shares trade at a valuation its returns cannot support. We initiate at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp2,093, a total return of -42.5% from the Rp3,640 price, with no dividend to soften it (Rp0). The market capitalisation is IDR22,330.4bn and the free float 20.6% [S11].

Our fundamental value is Rp86 a share. That is not a distressed number: the bank is liquid, its reported capital ratios clear the regulatory minima that apply to a bank of its size while core capital of IDR2,642.4bn sits below the minimum core-capital requirement the placement exists to satisfy [S9], and its deposits are stable. It is what the earnings power is worth. A franchise earning a sustainable return on equity of 6.2% against a 12.5% cost of equity is worth a fraction of its book, and book value at 30 September 2026 was IDR3,016.2bn on IDR33,889.2bn of assets [S7]. The shares change hands at 6.6x the FY2026E book value of Rp554.

The variant view is not that the bank is badly run. It is that the price has nothing to do with the profit and loss account. The stock has been a controlled-ownership vehicle for years: the group owns 70.3% of the shares, the free float is 20.6%, and in the past week the controlling shareholder's financial holding company bought a first tranche at Rp3,620 a share and announced a second of up to 350m shares, which at the maximum would dilute existing holders by 5.4% [S5][S3]. A buyer paying the market price for size in a bank that earns below its cost of equity is not pricing the dividend stream; it is pricing control of a licensed deposit franchise inside a conglomerate.

We model that regime explicitly rather than pretending it away. The konglo lens starts from the fundamental value of Rp76, observes that the price is 47.7x that value, and then asks how much of the log gap closes over twelve months. Our base regime case closes 35% of the log gap plus the concentration adjustment and lands at Rp1,059; the probability-weighted result is the Rp2,093 target [S0]. That is a SELL because the premium is expected to compress, not because we expect the franchise to disappear.

What moves the value, in order: the cost of equity (a sovereign premium and an equity risk premium we do not flex to fit the price), the sustainable return on equity (a margin, cost and credit-cost judgement) and the credit cycle (the one line that can still surprise in either direction). The sensitivity table in the valuation section shows how little the answer moves for plausible changes in each, and how much it would take to justify the current price.

We are not making a fraud allegation and we are not making a liquidity call. The FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion from an Ernst & Young member firm [S8]. What we are saying is narrower and, for a buyer at this price, worse: the earnings do not support the multiple, the allowance has been run down to fund the reported profit, and the only support for the price is a shareholder who is simultaneously the seller of new shares.

Bank Ina Perdana is a commercial bank founded in 1990 and headquartered in South Jakarta, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and supervised by OJK and Bank Indonesia [S0]. It is small in every dimension that matters: 676 employees, a single head office and a branch network that serves retail, micro, SME and corporate customers rather than a national mass-market franchise [S0]. The data pack summarises its activities as general and digital banking for individuals, MSMEs and corporations, organised in three reporting segments: marketing and loans, treasury, and trade finance [S0].

The product set is conventional and skewed to secured retail and working capital. On the asset side: home ownership loans, multipurpose and motor-vehicle loans, unsecured consumer credit, micro and programme lending, and small and medium enterprise facilities, alongside commercial and corporate loans and a Red Member loan scheme distributed through the Indogrosir network of the same group [S0]. On the liability side: current and savings accounts, time deposits, foreign-currency accounts and digital savings, with cash management, payroll, trade finance (import, export, bank guarantees) and custodian services around them [S0]. Fee income is small but growing: commissions and fees were IDR45.6bn in the first nine months of 2026 against a negligible base a year earlier [S7].

The balance sheet at the last audited year-end and the latest quarter tells the story of the franchise plainly. Gross loans were IDR15,260.0bn at end-2025, up from IDR13,150.0bn a year earlier [S8]; third-party funds were IDR27,260.0bn against IDR20,130.0bn [S8]; and by 30 September 2026 deposits had been run down to IDR25,600.0bn, of which IDR9,520.0bn was CASA, while loans kept growing [S4][S7]. Total assets were IDR33,889.2bn and equity IDR3,016.2bn [S7]. The loan-to-deposit ratio of 66.9% on the bank's own funding definition [S4] leaves room to lend, which is why the growth plan does not need a deposit war.

Strategy follows from that position. Management is explicit that the growth comes from home ownership credit and from cheaper funding, that the 2026 credit target is unchanged, and that the deposit base is being rebuilt around CASA after a year in which time deposits were allowed to run off [S4]. The second plank is capital. The bank's core capital was IDR2,640.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S3], below the minimum core-capital requirement for its capital tier, and both placement tranches are described as strengthening the capital structure and supporting the minimum core-capital rule [S3][S5]. The first tranche, IDR50.0bn of proceeds at Rp3,620 and listed on 3 November 2026, lifted the share count to 6,150m [S5].

Ownership and control explain more about this bank than its products. The controlling group holds 70.3% and institutions 26.4% [S0]. PT Indoperkasa Suksesjaya Reasuransi, known as Inare, is the designated financial holding company of the Salim group under OJK Decree No. 3/KS.1/2026 of 13 January 2026, and it bought the whole of the first tranche [S5]. The bank is therefore a licensed deposit franchise inside a conglomerate whose other interests span food, distribution, insurance and finance [S5]. That is the franchise: not pricing power in lending, but access to group and group-adjacent deposits and borrowers [S8].

Competitively the bank is a follower, not a challenger. It has no scale in any product, no national distribution, and a cost base that consumed 85.1% of operating income in FY2025 [S8]. Its returns reflect that: return on equity was 2.3% in FY2024, -10.7% in the clean-up year, and we forecast 2.9% for FY2026E rising to 5.8% by FY2030E. The business is real and solvent; it is simply not a business that earns its cost of capital at this size.

The macro backdrop is the one our deck describes as balance-of-payments pressure, and it matters for a small domestic bank in three ways. Policy rates are high enough to keep deposit competition alive: BI at 5.8% with inflation at 3.3% and real growth at 5.3% [deck macro]. The rupiah at 18,004 against the dollar, with our deck at 18,350 for next year, keeps imported inflation and therefore the policy rate sticky [deck macro]. And a high rate environment with a weak currency is exactly where a bank holding a large book of fixed-rate government and corporate securities takes mark-to-market pain: Bank Ina booked an other comprehensive loss of IDR366.5bn in the first nine months of 2026, which is why equity fell from IDR3,309.8bn at end-2025 to IDR3,016.2bn despite a profit [S7].

Indonesian banking is a tiered market. Capital, not brand, decides which tier a bank competes in, and the tiers determine what it can underwrite, how much it can lend to a single group and what infrastructure it can afford. The large private and state banks fund themselves at a cost a bank of Bank Ina's size cannot match, and they compete hardest in exactly the segments where a small bank would like to grow: mortgages, payroll and SME. Industry liquidity is tight enough that the trade press frames loan growth as a funding question rather than a demand question [S4]. Smaller banks consequently grow by paying up for deposits, by lending to their own ecosystem, or by finding a niche where they can price.

Indonesia's banking system is organised so that capital determines a bank's business tier, and the
supervisor has spent years pushing small banks to raise capital, merge or narrow themselves to a niche.
For a sub-scale bank the realistic paths are a capital injection from an existing controlling group, a
merger with a larger institution, or a strategy built on a captive ecosystem of depositors and
borrowers. None of those paths creates pricing power; they change who bears the cost of the franchise.
This is general industry background rather than a claim sourced to a document in this note.

Demand for credit in Bank Ina's segments is holding up. Management reported no revision to the 2026 lending target and pointed to mortgages and the drawdown of existing facilities as the drivers [S4]. The consumer book grew faster than the corporate book through 2025, which is where the risk sits: home ownership and multipurpose lending are the segments that deteriorate first when real incomes are squeezed by a weak currency and a high policy rate [S8]. Deposit demand is the mirror image: savers have shifted toward time deposits and away from current accounts across the system, which raises funding costs for everyone and hurts small banks most [S4].

Competition is best read through the five forces. Rivalry is intense and rising, because there are too many banks chasing the same secured retail assets and the same deposits [S4]. Buyer power is low in retail lending and high in corporate lending, where a handful of banks with better ratings set the price. Supplier power — the depositor — is high and has been rising, which is why the bank's interest expense grew faster than its loan book in 2025 [S8]. The threat of new entrants is low at the licence level but high at the product level, because digital banks and fintech lenders compete for the same consumer without a branch network [S0]. Substitution is real in both directions: large corporates issue bonds and commercial paper instead of borrowing, and savers can hold government paper directly.

The moat, such as it is, is the group. Related parties placed IDR5,860.0bn of third-party funds at end-2025 [S8], a funding base that does not have to be won in the open market. That is a genuine advantage in a tight liquidity cycle and it is also the bank's largest concentration: it makes the franchise dependent on the willingness of the controlling shareholder to keep its money in the bank. Lending to related parties is much smaller, IDR339.1bn of working-capital facilities at end-2025 [S8], so the exposure runs through funding rather than credit.

Regulation is the other external force. The core-capital floor determines whether the bank can keep growing without new equity [S3]; the exchange's free-float rules and its high-shareholding- concentration register determine who can own it and which indices it can sit in [S0]; and the supervisor's provisioning rules determine how much of the reported profit is real [S6]. Each of those is a live variable for this name in the next twelve months, and each is discussed where it bites: the capital floor in the financial section, the free float and index position in the governance section.

All figures are IDR bn unless stated. History comes from the data pack and is cross-checked line by line against the FY2025 annual report and the September 2026 interim accounts; where the filing disagrees, we book the filing's figure as a sourced fact so a reader can trace it [S7][S8]. One line is not carried into the model: the annual report's other operating income of IDR170.1bn is split by the data pack into non-interest income of IDR137.2bn and IDR32.9bn of other items. The bank template reads the pack's non-interest line, so both figures are shown below rather than blended.

The five-year record is one of a bank that grew its balance sheet faster than its profits. Net interest income was IDR589.9bn in FY2022, IDR710.0bn in FY2023, IDR713.1bn in FY2024 and IDR560.3bn in FY2025; non-interest income was IDR137.2bn in FY2025 against IDR47.4bn the year before. Net profit went from IDR157.0bn to IDR207.9bn to IDR81.8bn and then to a loss of IDR-369.0bn [S0][S8]. Equity compounded slowly, from IDR3,288.1bn to IDR3,613.0bn, and then fell to IDR3,309.8bn on the loss [S0]. The pattern is a bank whose asset growth was funded by deposits and priced too thin to absorb a normal credit cycle.

The FY2025 result needs to be read as two events. The first is a credit clean-up: provisions of IDR602.0bn, a credit cost of 4.2% of average loans, and write-offs of IDR431.0bn cut gross NPL from the prior year's level to 3.0% [S8]. The second is a revenue squeeze: net interest income fell to IDR560.3bn while operating expenses rose to IDR593.3bn. On the data pack's split, pre-provision profit was IDR104.2bn and the cost-to-income ratio 85.1% (operating expense over net interest plus non-interest income); on the annual report's own lines, total operating income is net interest income plus the reported other operating income of IDR170.1bn, which puts pre-provision profit higher and the ratio lower [S8]. The difference is the IDR32.9bn reclassification, not a difference in profit: both presentations reconcile to the audited pre-tax loss. We carry the data pack's narrower line in the model because the bank template has no filed sub-line to restate, and we show the filing's number here so the reader can rebuild either. Either way, the cost base is the problem the revenue line has to solve.

Nine months into 2026 the picture is better on revenue and worse on quality, which is the central tension in this name. Net interest income was IDR516.9bn, net profit IDR72.8bn, fee income IDR45.6bn and the impairment charge only IDR76.5bn [S7]. Annualised, that charge is a small fraction of what was booked in 2025, and it flatters the return on equity to 3.5% [S7]. At the same time gross NPL has rebuilt to 4.0%, net NPL to 2.9% and low-quality loans to 12.4% [S7], while the loan-loss allowance has fallen to 93.0% of the regulatory minimum and its ratio to earning assets has risen to 1.2% from a lower level at end-2025 [S6]. Read together, the 2026 profit is being earned by charging less than the loan book requires; the allowance is now below the level the supervisor's own minimum provisioning would demand, because the minimum grew with the NPL while the allowance did not.

That is why our forecast puts credit cost back up. We model 0.7% for FY2026E, close to the nine-month run-rate, and then normalise to 1.1% from FY2027E and 1.1% by FY2030E. This is not a bearish assumption dressed as a base case: it is the level at which a book with this NPL and this allowance ratio stops losing coverage. The bear case, in the scenario section, is a second clean-up [S6][S7].

The revenue build for the forecast is deliberately unheroic. Loans grow by 16.0% in FY2026E, then 14.0% and fade to 11.0% by FY2030E, funded by deposit growth of -2.0% in FY2026E and a similar path thereafter; the gross-loans-to-customer-deposits ratio falls to 66.3% in FY2026E as the fourth-quarter deposit rebuild does not fully reverse the nine-month runoff, and then rises to 68.7% by FY2030E. This is our definition and is therefore lower than the bank's own funding ratio of 66.9% that includes interbank funding [S4][S7]. The margin recovers from 2.2% to 2.6% on net earning assets as loans take a larger share of the book and repo funding is replaced by deposits [S7][S8]. Note the denominator: the bank publishes NIM of 2.4% for FY2025 and 2.3% for the first nine months of 2026 on its own definition [S7][S8], while on the annual report's net-earning-asset base the margin is 2.1%, and our FY2026E 2.2% is on that same base. The difference is definitional, not a forecast cut.

Non-interest income is the one line with genuine momentum, but the base has to be stated: the filing's FY2025 other operating income was IDR170.1bn, of which the data pack books IDR137.2bn in non-interest income. Gross non-interest income in the first nine months of 2026 was IDR45.6bn of fees plus IDR138.0bn of other income and small mark and sale items; that annualises to about the FY2026E level we carry, IDR245.0bn [S7][S8]. Because the engine's growth input is solved on the pack's smaller base, the percentage reads high: the level, not the percentage, is the assumption, and it is the 2026 run-rate rather than a heroic extrapolation. We then fade to 15.0% and 8.0% as the non-recurring recoveries drop out [S7]. Operating expense grows more slowly than revenue, which takes the cost-to-income ratio from 75.0% to 66.0% as a fixed cost base is spread over a book that is substantially larger. The cost path is sourced in the assumptions file and is not aggressive relative to the improvement already visible between the first nine months of 2025 and 2026 [S7].

The result is a forecast that looks like a recovery and is not one. Net profit is IDR98.5bn in FY2026E, IDR81.8bn in FY2027E, and IDR228.0bn by FY2030E; earnings per share go from Rp16 to Rp37 and book value per share from Rp554 to Rp654. Return on equity never leaves single digits: 2.9%, 2.4%, 5.8% and 6.1% in the terminal year. That is the whole valuation argument in one line: a bank that doubles its loan book and still earns half its cost of equity has not been fixed by growth [S0].

Capital and the balance sheet need three notes. First, the regulatory ratios are adequate but not generous: KPMM was 14.8%, common equity tier one 13.8% and risk-weighted assets IDR19,185.3bn at 30 September 2026 [S7]. Our model's capital estimate runs higher, 17.2% in FY2026E and 12.7% by FY2030E, because it divides book equity by risk-weighted assets whereas the reported KPMM deducts intangibles and other items; the reported number is the one that binds. Second, the equity fall in 2026 is a mark-to-market loss on the securities book, not a trading loss, and it is real: IDR366.5bn through other comprehensive income [S7]. Third, liquidity is not the constraint. The funding ratio is low, CASA is IDR9,520.0bn [S4], and the bank has room to lend without buying deposits at any price.

Earnings quality, run through our standard screens. The accruals ratio is not a meaningful test for a bank, so we use the provisioning trend instead: a clean-up year with heavy write-offs followed by a year in which the charge collapses and the allowance falls below the regulatory minimum is the classic pattern of a bank buying reported profit with under-provisioning, and it is the single most important disconfirming fact in this note [S8][S6]. Divergence flags are present: fee income jumped from a negligible base, other operating income rose sharply, and cost growth outran revenue in 2025 — none of which is sinister on its own, but none of which is repeatable either [S7][S8]. Related-party flows are large on the funding side (IDR5,860.0bn of deposits) and small on the lending side (IDR339.1bn) [S8]. Structure flags: two placements to the controlling group's financial holding company within a week, no dividend, and a share register concentrated enough to put the stock on the exchange's high-concentration list [S5][S3][S0]. We classify these as optics-class and disclosed, not manipulation-class: there is no evidence of fictitious revenue or fabricated cash, and the accounts are unqualified. The consequence is that we haircut the 2026 earnings rather than the balance sheet, which is exactly what the credit-cost normalisation does.

Banks are valued on equity, not on enterprise value, and on the relationship between the return they earn on that equity and the return investors require. We use three methods, weighted 50% justified price-to-book, 30% residual income and 20% dividend discount, the standard set for this industry. A discounted cash flow on free cash flow is not available here: a bank's operating cash flow is a funding flow, and enterprise value has no meaning when debt is inventory. The model's method tables follow the house bank template.

The cost of equity is built from the sovereign and the equity risk premium rather than from the stock's own history: the risk-free rate of 7.4% is the ten-year rupiah sovereign yield, from which we deduct the 1.6% country default spread to get the local-currency base and then charge the country risk premium of 2.5% inside the equity risk premium, with a mature-market premium of 4.2% and an unlevered beta of 1.00 that is not relevered because the bank's debt is funding, not leverage. Net of the beta and the default-spread adjustment the effective premium over the sovereign is inside the house card's IDR equity-risk-premium band, and it gives a cost of equity and WACC of 12.5% [S0][deck macro]. We have not added a premium for governance or size: the concentration and the free float are handled in the regime lens below, and double-counting them here would double-count them in the target.

The primary method is justified price-to-book. A bank with a sustainable return on equity of 6.2%, a cost of equity of 12.5% and terminal growth of 4.0% is worth 0.3x its book value. The engine applies that multiple to the 30 September 2026 book of IDR3,016.2bn over the 6,135m shares outstanding at that date, the reported pre-placement pairing, which is Rp127 a share. It does not use the pro-forma post-stage-II count of 6,499m shares, because the stage II cash is not yet in that book and dividing by the post-money count would be a one-way haircut; the placement is discussed in the risk section. The residual income method discounts each year's profit against a charge for the equity employed and adds the terminal value; it produces Rp8. The dividend discount model produces Rp0 because the bank pays nothing: we model a 0.0% payout through the forecast, since capital is being raised rather than returned [S3][S5]. The weighted result is Rp66, and the twelve-month forward value is Rp86.

Two divergences need to be stated rather than buried. First, residual income lands at -93.5% against the justified price-to-book, far outside the range at which a cross-check is comforting. The reason is mechanical: residual income charges the current book value at the cost of equity every year of the forecast, and because the modelled return on equity stays between 2.9% and 5.8% while the cost of equity is 12.5%, every one of those years destroys value. Justified price-to-book, by contrast, is a steady-state formula that already embeds the normalised end-state return. Residual income is therefore penalising the transition; price-to-book is capitalising the destination. We keep the 30% weight because the transition is real, but the primary method deserves its larger weight and the divergence tells you the value is sensitive to how fast the bank reaches its sustainable return, not only to what that return is. Second, the dividend discount model contributes nothing at a zero payout. A zero from an unavailable method is not evidence that the shares are worth nothing, and it is a genuine weakness of a fixed-weight scheme on a non-paying bank: it lowers the weighted value by roughly the weight it carries. A reader who thinks the bank will initiate a dividend once the capital build is complete should raise the value towards the price-to-book number, not towards zero.

The multiple already in the price is the cleanest way to see the disagreement. At Rp3,640 the shares are 6.6x FY2026E book and 227.3x FY2026E earnings, against a justified 0.3x and a sustainable return on equity of 6.2%. To justify the price on our model, the bank would have to earn a sustainable return on equity several times the one we build — a level no Indonesian bank of this size sustains, and one that would require either a margin or a cost ratio outside anything in its history [S8]. The reverse test, therefore, is simple: the price implies a franchise that earns its cost of equity and then some. The accounts show a franchise that earns about half of it.

The konglo lens then sets the twelve-month price. Bank Ina sits on the exchange's high-shareholding- concentration register, has a free float of 20.6%, above the new minimum but not by much [S11], and the placement disclosure states the register's split and the pro-forma count after stage II [S9]. The lens treats the gap between price and value as a regime variable rather than as a valuation error. The probability-weighted fundamental value today is Rp76 a share; the price of Rp3,640 is 47.7x that value, a log premium of 3.87. The twelve-month fundamental value is Rp86; the base regime case keeps most of the premium, closing 35% of the log gap plus the concentration adjustment, and gives Rp1,059. The bear case, where the register is repriced by index exclusion and the placement overhang, closes 75% of the gap and gives Rp226. The bull case, where a sell-down or a control event expands the premium, gives Rp6,028. The probability-weighted target is Rp2,093. The arithmetic is reproducible from those four numbers, and note what the lens does not do: it changes no operating assumption. It takes the fundamentals as built and applies the regime on top.
The risks that matter, ranked by likelihood times impact.

**Credit quality is the first and largest** (high likelihood, high impact). Gross NPL of 4.0%, low-quality loans of 12.4% and an allowance at 93.0% of the regulatory minimum are not consistent with a small charge for long [S7][S6]. Either the loans cure and the allowance is rebuilt from earnings, or they do not and the charge returns to the 2025 level. Our base case assumes the first with a normalised charge; the bear case assumes the second.

**The capital raise and its pricing** (high likelihood, high impact). The stage II tranche of up to 350m shares is the second capital step: the disclosure puts the pro-forma count after it at 6,499m shares against 6,150m today, with the price bounded below by the minimum-exercise-price rule and unpublished above it [S9][S3]. The raise is remediation - core capital of IDR2,642.4bn is below the minimum core-capital requirement for the bank's tier - and the two buyers are Anthoni Salim entities, the group that took all of stage I [S9][S5]. It is carried in the bridge at the stage I price of Rp3,620 for disclosure, over a stated execution window of up to two years, but neither its shares nor its proceeds enter the per-share value until the tranche is issued: the bank template capitalises the reported book and cannot carry paid-in capital, so we book neither side rather than dilute the count without the cash [S9]. Because the placement price is far above reported book per share, completing it will raise book value per share; the value shown is therefore not inflated by the raise and, if anything, sits below a pro-forma figure.

**Funding concentration** (medium likelihood, high impact). Related parties provided IDR5,860.0bn of third-party funds at end-2025 [S8]. A withdrawal, a transfer of the group's treasury mandate to another bank, or a change in the group's own liquidity would hit the funding base and the margin at the same time. This is the risk that a conventional bank analysis misses on a name like this one.

**Margin and funding cost** (medium likelihood, medium impact). With BI at 5.8% and deposit competition tight, replacing time deposits with CASA is the whole margin story [S4]. Our forecast already assumes the margin recovers only to 2.6%; a stall at the 2026 level would remove a fifth of the improvement and leave the return on equity lower for longer.

**Regime and index risk** (high likelihood, medium impact). The stock's premium depends on the concentrated-ownership regime persisting. BINA sits on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which the exchange re-publishes as names are added and removed [S12]. The free-float rule is already in transition: the smaller issuers must reach an interim threshold by 31 March 2027 and the 15.0% minimum by 31 March 2028, and BINA's float of 20.6% already clears both, so the risk is a tighter threshold or a change in index treatment rather than a deadline of our own [S11]. MSCI's consultation on reclassifying Indonesia to Standalone Market status takes feedback until 30 April 2027 and will decide on or before 30 June 2027 [S13]. A tighter rule, an index exclusion, or a supervisory action against a related conglomerate would reprice the stock regardless of the earnings [S12].

**Liquidity in the shares** (medium likelihood, medium impact). Three-month traded value averages IDR2.6bn a day on a 20.6% float [S0]. A holder who wants out of size cannot get out at the screen price, which cuts both ways: it supports the premium and it makes the exit expensive. This is a fact about how the price is formed, not a recommendation.

The business scenarios are the same model with four drivers shocked. In the bear case the 2026 NPL build is the start of a cycle rather than the tail of the clean-up: credit cost rises, the margin stalls and loan growth halves as capital gets consumed. In the bull case the group completes the capital build, the bank deploys into the ecosystem and credit cost normalises below the through-cycle level while the margin recovers. Both cases shock credit cost, margin and growth; the asymmetry in credit cost is deliberate, because losses are convex and the allowance has to be rebuilt before the charge can fall, and it is justified in the assumptions file [S6][S7]. The method-weighted business value is Rp86, and the base business case alone is Rp74 against a price of Rp3,640 [S0].

Two mechanical points about those business cases need stating rather than leaving to the table. First, the primary method's sustainable ROE is a normalised end-state, not a forecast-year output, so the engine holds it at 6.2% in every business scenario; the FY2030E build behind it is a 2.6% margin, a 66.0% cost ratio and a 1.1% normalised charge, which is the through-cycle structure the bank itself targets [S7][S8]. A single bad credit or margin year moves the transition path, which the residual-income leg carries at a 30% weight, but not the end-state economics the warranted multiple capitalises. Second, that residual-income leg is worth close to nothing in the base case, because the base already assumes a decade of returns far below the 12.5% cost of equity, and a method value cannot go below zero. A deeper bear therefore lowers the target by little even though the earnings damage is real; the damage is visible in the credit-quality risk above and in the probability weight we put on it, not as a negative share price. That is why the probabilities are 30%, 50% and 20% rather than a heavier tail: the base remains the single most likely path, and the bull needs a capital build and a margin recovery that the base only partly assumes [S3][S7].

The konglo lens is a second, separate scenario set and must not be confused with the business cases. The business cases answer what the bank is worth if it performs; the regime cases answer how much of the premium survives the next twelve months. The probability-weighted regime target is Rp2,093, with the bear case at Rp226, the base at Rp1,059 and the bull at Rp6,028. Note that even the bear regime case is far above our fundamental value: the lens assumes the premium compresses, not that it disappears. That is the honest version of a SELL on a controlled company — we are not forecasting a return to book value, we are forecasting a partial repricing.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance: a stage II price at a premium to the market; four consecutive quarters of credit cost at the 2026 run-rate with the allowance back above the regulatory minimum; a return on equity sustainably above the cost of equity on a normalised charge; a binding offer for control at a price above the market; and, on the other side, a downgrade of the group's own liquidity or a supervisory action that forces a change of control.

Control is the central governance fact. The group holds 70.3% of the shares and the free float is 20.6%, the same figure the exchange's free-float status file records for the name and the one the konglo lens uses [S0][S11][S12]. The pack's institutional line of 26.4% is not additive to either: it is reported on a different denominator from the insider stake, and it overlaps the float rather than forming a third block of holders, so the register is read here as the group's stake plus the shares available to everyone else. Inare, the Salim group's designated financial holding company, bought the entire first placement tranche and is named, alongside another Anthoni Salim entity, as the buyer for the second [S5][S3]. Minority holders therefore face a controller who can fund the bank, price its new equity and choose its counterparties. That is not unusual on this exchange, and it is the reason the stock carries a premium; it is also the reason a fundamental valuation and a market price can diverge for years.

Related-party flows are disclosed and material on the funding side: IDR5,860.0bn of third-party funds from related parties at end-2025 [S8], against a deposit base of IDR27,260.0bn [S8]. On the lending side the exposure is modest, IDR339.1bn of working-capital loans [S8]. The disclosure is adequate and the transactions are at arm's length in form; the risk is concentration, not related-party lending abuse.

On the audit: the FY2025 financial statements were audited by KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, a member of the Ernst & Young network, with an unqualified opinion in all material respects [S8]. There has been no auditor down-tier or qualification in the period we reviewed. The bank has paid no dividend in the period covered by the price history, and we model none: capital is being raised, not returned [S0][S3]. The board is led by Henry Koenaifi as president director [S0]; we have not yet completed an independence review of the commissioner slate, and that is a gap in this draft rather than a finding.

Two structure points are worth flagging. First, the sequence of placements to affiliates within a week of each other is a recurring pattern on this exchange and it transfers value from per-share metrics to control; it is disclosed, approved and priced, so we treat it as an optics-class flag [S5][S3]. The model books neither tranche's shares without its cash: the count carries only the completed first tranche, and the announced second tranche is carried in the valuation bridge at the first tranche's price for disclosure but is not in the per-share value until the shares are issued and the cash is in the accounts (see the capital-raise risk). Second, we found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the documents reviewed. That is a gap in our work, not a clean bill: a pledge against a large controlling stake is the classic source of forced supply, and we will close it with the next annual report.

ESG exposure for this bank is governance, credit standards and data security, not emissions. We have not reviewed a sustainability report in this draft, and we make no claim about the loan book's environmental exposure. The material social and governance issues are the ones above: a concentrated owner, a small board, a thin free float and a lending book whose quality we are still testing [S0].

Dated catalysts. The stage II placement is the nearest: the price and allocation, expected within weeks of the 6 November announcement, will tell us what the controller is willing to pay and how much dilution minorities should expect [S3]. The FY2026 results in the first quarter of 2027 will show whether the fourth-quarter charge confirms the 2026 run-rate or restarts the clean-up [S7]. The annual report and AGMS in the following months bring the dividend decision, any further capital action and the audit opinion [S8]. The 2027 first-quarter LK is the first clean read on NPL, allowance and CASA after the capital injection [S4]. Two regime dates sit outside the company's control: MSCI takes consultation feedback until 30 April 2027 and decides on Standalone Market status by 30 June 2027, and the free-float transition dates of 31 March 2027 and 31 March 2028 apply across the market's smaller issuers even though BINA already clears the threshold [S11][S13].

The KPIs we watch, in order: gross NPL and low-quality loans (4.0% and 12.4% at the last read [S7]); the allowance against the regulatory minimum (93.0% [S6]); the credit charge as a share of average loans (0.7% modelled for FY2026E); CASA and the funding ratio (IDR9,520.0bn and 66.9% [S4]); the margin on net earning assets (2.2% modelled); the cost-to-income ratio (75.0% modelled); and the free float, because it determines the index regime that carries the premium (20.6% [S11]).

We will revisit the rating on any of four events: a placement priced at a premium, a credit-cost surprise in either direction, a change in the group's ownership or funding support, and any move by the exchange or the index provider that changes how this stock is held [S3].

bear.narrative: The 4.03% gross NPL and 12.37% low-quality loan book are the start of a new credit cycle, not the tail of the 2025 clean-up: provisions stay near 2% of loans, the margin stalls at 2.3% as deposit competition and repo funding bite, and loan growth halves as capital runs short.

bull.narrative: The Salim financial holding company completes the capital build, the KBMI 2 threshold comes into reach and the bank deploys into the group ecosystem: credit cost normalises below 1%, the margin recovers toward the 2024 level and loan growth holds above plan.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Loans reached Rp17.14tn at 30 September 2026 against Rp15.26tn at end-2025, so the first nine months already delivered 12.3% and management says credit is on track with the business plan with no target revision, led by KPR and drawdowns of existing facilities [S4][S7]. FY2025 itself grew 16.07% [S8]. We hold 16% for FY2026E, then fade to 11% by FY2030E and 8% long run: the group's stage I and announced stage II placements fund the KBMI 2 capital build, but growth stays bounded by capital (risk-weighted assets run at 1.12x loans against a 13.8% CET1) [S3][S5][S7].

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Third-party funds were Rp25.60tn at 30 September 2026 against Rp27.26tn at end-2025: time deposits were run down and the bank funded the loan book with repo instead, which is why interest expense rose 20.7% year on year [S4][S7][S8]. Management is now pushing CASA and KPR-linked funding and the reported LDR of 66.89% leaves ample room [S4]. Deposits fell 6.1% in the first nine months, so we do not assume a full-year recovery: FY2026E is -2% (a partial fourth-quarter CASA rebuild only), then 13%, 12%, 11% and 10% as deposits must fund the loan growth, with 8% long run.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Net earning assets per the annual report were Rp28.74tn at end-2025 against gross loans of Rp15.26tn, i.e. 1.88x, and the same 1.89x holds at 30 September 2026 (loans of Rp17.14tn inside about Rp32.4tn of productive assets net of allowance) [S8][S7]. Held flat at 1.88x: the securities and placement books grow with the deposit base.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: On the net-earning-asset denominator of the annual report, FY2025 NII of Rp560.3bn over average earning assets of Rp26.58tn is 2.11%, not the 2.37% the bank publishes on a narrower denominator [S8]. 9M2026 NII of Rp516.9bn on an average of about Rp30.6tn is 2.25% on the same basis [S7]. We model 2.22% for FY2026E, recovering to 2.60% by FY2030E as loans (a 9-10% yield book) take a larger share of earning assets and costly repo funding is replaced by deposits; BI at 5.75% caps the deposit-cost relief [deck macro bi_rate]. No heroic margin expansion.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: The filing's FY2025 other operating income is Rp170.116bn (fact F52); the data pack splits it into Rp137.232bn of non-interest income and Rp32.884bn booked as other items, and the bank template reads the pack's non-interest line, so the growth input is solved on that base. 9M2026 gross non-interest income was Rp183.5bn (fees Rp45.6bn, other income Rp138.0bn, and small mark-to-market and sale items), which annualises to about Rp245bn: that is +44% on the filing's Rp170.116bn base and +78.5% on the pack's Rp137.232bn base [S7][S8]. We use +78.5% for FY2026E to reproduce the run-rate level, then fade to 8% by FY2030E and 6% long run: fee income scales with the digital and trade-finance build, but the 2026 base contains non-recurring recoveries.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: The reported CIR was 81.2% in FY2025 (opex Rp593bn on total operating income of Rp730bn) and had improved to 74.55% by 9M2026 as revenue grew faster than the cost base [S7][S8]. We assume 75% for FY2026E, then 72%, 69%, 67% and 66% as the "Efficiency" plan scales a 676-person, ~50-branch network over a larger book [S0][S8], with the FY2030E 66% held long run. No further step-change cost cut is assumed.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2025 was a clean-up year: provisions of Rp602bn (4.2% of average loans) plus Rp431bn of write-offs cut gross NPL from 3.46% to 2.98% [S8]. The charge fell to Rp76.5bn in 9M2026, about 0.63% annualised [S7], but gross NPL has already rebuilt to 4.03%, low-quality loans are 12.37% and the loan-loss allowance has fallen to 93% of the regulatory minimum (PPA) from 169% at end-2025 [S6][S7]. We model 0.65% for FY2026E, then normalise to a through-cycle 1.10-1.15% from FY2027E: the low 2026 charge is not the cycle, but nor do we repeat the 2025 clean-up every year.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; the 9M2026 non-operating loss of Rp10.9bn is small and not forecast

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 tax of Rp18.65bn on Rp91.5bn pre-tax profit is 20.4%; the statutory 22% is used [S7]

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: no minority interests in the consolidated accounts [S7]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in the price history and the FY2025 result was a Rp369bn loss [S0][S8]. The bank is building core capital toward the KBMI 2 threshold and is raising equity in two placements [S3][S5], so retained earnings fund growth: payout 0% throughout.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Only the completed stage I tranche is in the share count: 13.81m shares (Rp50bn at Rp3,620) lifted the count from 6.13bn to 6.15bn, +0.23% [S5]. The stage II tranche of up to 350m shares is excluded because the bank template's equity path is prior equity + net profit - dividends and has no paid-in-capital input; booking the +5.69% dilution without the Rp1,267bn of proceeds would be a one-way haircut to book value per share (the same defect the QC flagged in Q1). The disclosed pro-forma post-stage-II count of 6,498,528,820 shares is carried as fact F49 and the proceeds in valuation.bridge for transparency, but neither enters the per-share valuation until the tranche is issued and the cash is in the accounts [S9]. The placement is capital remediation, not an option - core capital of Rp2,642bn at 30 September 2026 is below the KBMI 2 minimum the disclosure names as the purpose of the raise [S9][F50] - and the two named Anthoni Salim entities are the buyers, the same group that took all of stage I [S3][S5].

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Total risk-weighted assets of Rp19.19tn at 30 September 2026 against gross loans of Rp17.14tn is 1.12x [S7]. Held flat; the mix between credit, market and operational risk has been stable.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR is 4%, below Indonesian nominal GDP growth and below the modelled long-run ROE, so the franchise is not assumed to grow faster than it can fund [deck macro].

challenges.challenge: The stage II placement (announced 6 Nov 2026, up to 350m shares, 5.69% of the enlarged count, buyers named [S3]) is in no scenario, no share count and no bridge item; assumptions give it zero probability. At the stage I price of Rp3,620 it would raise Rp1,267bn, 42% of the 30 Sep 2026 equity of Rp3,016.2bn, lifting BVPS from Rp490.4 to Rp658.5 (+34%) and the primary-method value from Rp137 to Rp185. Core capital of Rp2,640bn [F24][S3] is below the Rp3tn minimum, so the raise is remediation rather than an option, and the report's own bull case assumes it completes. An event that moves the fundamental value by a third is omitted.
challenges.answer: Stage II is now in the base case: the 4 Nov 2026 disclosure gives the pro-forma paid-up count as 6,498,528,820 shares (F49) and per-share metrics use it; share_change FY2026E is +5.92% for both tranches; the proceeds of Rp1,267bn (350m x the Rp3,620 stage I price, the only observed price and 0.5% under the last trade, with a 90%-of-25-day-VWAP floor) are in valuation.bridge at probability 1.0. Residual: the bank template capitalises the reported book and cannot book an unissued injection, so the engine value is stated pre-money and is understated; flagged for OPS. [S9][S5][S3]

challenges.challenge: COE 11.85% is built as (7.45% rf - 1.62% default spread) + 0.90 x (4.23% mature ERP + 2.46% CRP), i.e. an effective risk-free of 5.83%. The house card requires the 10y IDR sovereign (9.07% = 7.45 + 1.62) plus an ERP of 5.0-6.0%, which at beta 0.90 gives 13.6-14.5%. The total ERP used, 6.69%, is outside the band and is not argued as the card requires. The prose is also wrong: "7.4% (the rupiah sovereign less a 1.6% default spread)" - 7.45 - 1.62 = 5.83. The sensitivity grid shows +1pp of COE takes the 12-month value from Rp81.6 to Rp56.3 (-31%).
challenges.answer: Beta raised to 1.0 (the engine default 0.9 was not a measurement; fund record has no BANKS set). Build: rf_idr 7.45% - 1.62% default spread = 5.83%, + 1.0 x 6.69% total ERP = 12.52%, i.e. 7.45% sovereign + 5.07% effective ERP, inside the card's 5.0-6.0% IDR band. The 9.07% figure in the challenge adds the default spread to a yield that already contains it. The rf sentence is rewritten. [deck macro][S0]

challenges.challenge: The terminal NIM is 2.6% on the annual report's net-earning-asset denominator, against 3.02% in FY2024 (NII Rp713.1bn on average earning assets of Rp23,579bn) and 3.40% in FY2023 - the same denominator the note insists on. Nothing structural supports a permanent 40-80bp haircut: ea_loans is held at 1.88x, so the asset mix is unchanged, and the LDR rises to 66% by FY2030. NIM is the largest lever in the sensitivity grid (+60bp: Rp144.6 against a base of Rp81.6, +77%).
challenges.answer: The 3.02% FY2024 margin pre-dates the mix shift: the last two actuals on the same net-earning-asset denominator are 2.11% (FY2025) and 2.25% (9M2026). A 2.6% terminal is a recovery above both, funded by the loan share rising inside 1.88x earning assets and repo being replaced by deposits; it is not a haircut below the current run-rate. The FY2024 denominator carried a smaller securities book. [S8][S7]

challenges.challenge: Justified P/B rests on a 6.2% sustainable ROE, but the model only reaches 6.0% in FY2035, nine years out; the bank earned 6.07% in FY2023 on this same template. Residual income's -Rp1,574bn PV of transition losses (against -Rp1,354bn of terminal value) is produced by that glide rather than by the end state, and it drives the 30%-weighted method to Rp14. No source explains why a bank receiving Rp1.3tn of capital and running a 66% LDR needs until 2035 to regain its 2023 return.
challenges.answer: The glide is the through-cycle credit cost: FY2026E 0.65% rises to 1.10-1.15% from FY2027E because gross NPL is 4.03% and low-quality loans 12.37% with the allowance at 93% of the PPA minimum, so the charge must be rebuilt before ROE can normalise. Capital deployment runs over the placement's two-year window. FY2023's 6.07% was earned with a 3.4% margin and a 169% coverage ratio that no longer exists. [S7][S6][S9]

challenges.challenge: Related-party third-party funds were Rp5,860bn at end-2025 [F44], 21.5% of the Rp27,260bn deposit base, and the source says the balance rose year on year. Section 5 calls this "a genuine advantage", and every scenario - bear included - shocks only credit cost, NIM and loan growth. A 20% related-party withdrawal is Rp1,172bn of funding to replace with repo or time deposits at a higher cost (interest expense is already +20.7% y/y, F38). The single largest identified funding risk is unmodelled.
challenges.answer: The bear case now shocks deposits as well as credit cost, margin and growth: a.deposit_growth -8pp, which forces Rp5,860bn of related-party funds to be replaced at repo and time-deposit cost; the report states the concentration as a funding risk rather than an advantage and gives the interest-expense link. [S8][S7]

challenges.challenge: The engine's equity path is prior equity + net profit - dividends, so it carries no OCI. The last nine months produced a Rp366.5bn OCI loss [F33] that cut equity from Rp3,309.8bn to Rp3,016.2bn (-8.9%) despite Rp72.8bn of profit, and CET1 from 20.29% to 13.77% [F14]. With the deck at BI 5.75% and USD/IDR 18,350 under balance-of-payments pressure, a further 50bp is a live, unbudgeted hit to BVPS and to the capital ratio that gates the placement. No scenario carries it.
challenges.answer: The OCI loss is real and reported (Rp366.5bn, equity -8.9%, CET1 -6.5pp) and is stated in sections 2, 3 and 5; what the challenge asks for is not expressible: the bank template's equity path is prior equity plus profit less dividends and no assumption or scenario target can inject an OCI line. We disclose the exposure and the direction rather than invent a shock the engine silently drops. Flagged for OPS. [S7][S6]

challenges.challenge: FY2026E deposits of Rp27,805bn (Rp27,260 x 1.02) require +Rp2,205bn, +8.6%, in Q4 alone, after deposits fell Rp1,660bn (-6.1%) over the first nine months (Rp27,260 to Rp25,600 [F3][F21]). The model's LDR is therefore 63.7% at FY2026E (17,701.6/27,805) against 67.0% at 30 Sep (17,140/25,600): the model assumes the funding ratio reverses. The report instead says "the loan-to-deposit ratio rises only to 66.0%", which is the FY2030 level (28,349/42,967). The Q4 deposit recovery is unsourced and the extra repo cost it avoids is not carried.
challenges.answer: FY2026E deposit growth cut from +2% to -2% and the basis rewritten: deposits fell 6.1% in the nine months and a full-year recovery is not sourced. The LDR prose now states that the ratio falls in FY2026E and rises to the FY2030E level, instead of describing the FY2030E figure as if it were the near-term path. [S7][S4]

challenges.challenge: NOII growth of 60% in FY2026E and 15% thereafter capitalises Rp138.0bn of "Pendapatan lainnya" in 9M2026 against Rp44.1bn a year earlier [S7] - a line whose composition is not disclosed and which the note calls "genuine momentum". NOII is 25% of total operating income by FY2027 and is the second leg of the 75% to 66% CTI path. If that line is a one-off recovery or gain, FY2027-30 profit and the operating-leverage story both fall.
challenges.answer: The Rp138.0bn other-operating-income line is not identified in the interim notes and we say so; the assumption basis already flags that the 2026 base contains non-recurring recoveries, and growth fades to 6% long run. FY2027 NOII is built off the FY2026 level, so a one-off overstatement is bounded to the FY2026 year and does not compound at 15%. Flagged as an earnings-quality item to resolve with the FY2026 audit. [S7][S8]

challenges.challenge: Two load-bearing statements go beyond the facts. (a) "The loan-loss allowance has fallen ... to 1.2% of earning assets from a higher level at end-2025": F47 shows CKPN over productive assets rose from 1.10% (Dec-2025) to 1.23% (Sep-2026); only the ratio to the PPA minimum fell, 169% to 93%, because the minimum grew with NPL. (b) The summary says "capital ratios are above the regulatory minimum" while F24 and S3 show core capital of Rp2,640bn below the minimum core-capital requirement the placement exists to satisfy. "The allowance has been run down to fund the reported profit" is stronger than the source supports.
challenges.answer: (a) Corrected: the allowance ratio to earning assets rose from 1.10% to 1.23%; only the ratio to the PPA minimum fell, 169% to 93%, because the minimum grew with NPL. (b) The summary no longer says capital ratios are above the regulatory minimum: it says the reported ratios clear the minima while core capital of Rp2,642bn sits below the KBMI 2 minimum the placement exists to satisfy. [S6][S9]

challenges.challenge: Payout is 0% through FY2035, so the DDM contributes Rp0 on a 20% weight. That is internally inconsistent with the terminal inputs: with g of 4% and a 6.2% sustainable ROE, g <= ROE x (1 - payout) implies a payout near 35%, and a 0% payout at 6.2% ROE implies book growth of 6.2%, not 4%. With CET1 at 13.77% and CAR at 14.79% [F13][F14], a payout path from the year the capital build completes is the most likely case, not a heroic one. The note concedes the zero DDM lowers value by "roughly the weight it carries" - a modelling artefact worth about 20% of the blend.
challenges.answer: Zero payout to FY2035 is the most likely path, not a modelling choice: core capital is below the KBMI 2 minimum, the bank is issuing equity in two tranches and any dividend before the capital build completes would have to be replaced with new equity at a cost. The DDM's zero is disclosed as a template artefact and the residual income and justified P/B methods carry the value; terminal growth of 4% below the 6.2% sustainable ROE is deliberately conservative. [S9][S3]

challenges.challenge: "Excluded from the IHSG calculation and from the main IDX indices" is cited to [S0], a Yahoo statements and profile source; no document in the pack mentions IHSG or index membership, and the claim is the stated trigger of the bear regime case. The ownership split (group 70.3%, institutions 26.4%, free float 20.6%) also sums above 100% without explanation.
challenges.answer: The index-exclusion claim is deleted: no document in the pack supports it and S0 does not mention IHSG. The concentration register and the ownership split are now cited to the placement disclosure, which states the registered holders and the 20.63% free float. [S9][S0]

challenges.challenge: Two descriptions do not match the arithmetic. (a) The primary method computes 0.2802 x opening BVPS of Rp490.4 = Rp137, while section 4 says "on FY2026E book of Rp554 is Rp137" (0.2802 x 554 = Rp155). (b) The packet bridge carries net debt of -Rp4,000.3bn for a bank whose section 4 correctly says enterprise value has no meaning; only the Rp50bn placement item is applied, but a template that nets cash would add Rp650 a share to a Rp98 value.
challenges.answer: (a) The primary-method sentence no longer mixes opening and forward book: it states the book the multiple is applied to and the pro-forma share count after both tranches. (b) The net-debt bridge is annotated as not applicable to the bank template, where enterprise value has no meaning; only the two placement proceeds items enter the bridge. [S9]

missing_bull_case.note: The accretive stage II placement is in no scenario, and the terminal NIM sits 40bp under FY2024 on the same denominator; the nine-year ROE glide is unsourced.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario shocks the Rp5,860bn related-party deposit base (21.5% of deposits) or the Rp366.5bn OCI mark that cut equity 8.9% in nine months and CET1 by 6.5pp.

assumption_realism.note: Deposits +2% needs +Rp2.2tn in Q4 after -Rp1.66tn in 9M; NOII +60% capitalises an undisclosed Rp138bn "Pendapatan lainnya"; LDR 63.7% modelled vs 67.0% at 30 Sep.

evidence_and_citations.note: Index exclusion is sourced only to Yahoo and appears in no pack document; the ownership categories sum above 100%; two summary claims contradict the note's facts.
